facts.text: In 1839 the French scientist Edmond Becquerel found that the electricity produced in his experiment increased when it was exposed to light.
In 1883 the American inventor Charles Fritts described the first solar cells, made from selenium.
Selenium cells could not turn enough sunlight into power to run electrical equipment.
In 1954 Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller and Gerald Pearson at Bell Labs made the first silicon solar cell able to run everyday electrical equipment.
The first Bell Labs silicon cell was about 4 percent efficient; later versions reached 11 percent.
Efforts to sell silicon solar cells in the 1950s and 1960s went poorly, but the cells were used successfully to power satellites.
In 1958 the Vanguard I satellite used a small array of solar cells (under one watt) to power its radios.
In 1963 Japan installed a 242-watt solar array on a lighthouse, the largest array in the world at that time.
